'''''Parmentiera aculeata''''' (synonym '''''Parmentiera edulis'''''), commonly known as '''cow okra''', '''cuajilote''', '''guajilote''', '''huachilote''', or '''pepino kat''', is a species of flowering tree in the family [[Bignoniaceae]]. It is native to Mexico and Central America and is known primarily for its edible fruit and medicinal properties.<ref name="Monaco">{{cite web |last1=Puccio |first1=Pietro |last2=Beltramini |first2=Mario |title=Parmentiera aculeata |url=https://www.monaconatureencyclopedia.com/parmentiera-aculeata/?lang=en |website=Monaco Nature Encyclopedia |access-date=13 June 2024 |date=9 June 2015}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The [[specific epithet]] (''aculeata'') is derived from [[Latin]] ''aculeatus'', which means "stinger", and refers to the thorns that are present on the [[Glossary of botanical terms#Node|nodes]] of young branches. The genus ''[[Parmentiera]]'' is named after French pharmacist and agronomist [[Antoine-Augustin Parmentier]].<ref name=Monaco/>

==Distribution==
''Parmentiera aculeata'' is native to central Mexico south to [[Nicaragua]]. It has been introduced to southern Central America, northern South America, and the [[Caribbean]], and is also cultivated in the United States, East Africa, [[Maritime Southeast Asia]], and Australia. It has become an [[invasive species]] in northern [[Queensland]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Areces-Berazain |first1=F. |title=Parmentiera aculeata (cucumber tree) |language=en |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.86635881 |date=7 January 2022|doi-access=free }}</ref>

It usually grows in dry to moist thickets and lowland forests, often near [[waterbodies]], typically at elevations around {{convert|1200|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}}, and prefers well-drained, sunny areas with medium to high rainfall.<ref name="Tropical">{{cite web |title=Parmentiera aculeata |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Parmentiera+aculeata |website=Useful Tropical Plants |access-date=11 June 2024}}</ref> It is hardy to [[USDA zones]] 10–12 and is not frost tolerant.<ref name="Desert">{{cite web |title=Guajilote, Cuachilote (Parmentiera edulis) |url=https://www.desert-tropicals.com/Plants/Bignoniaceae/Parmentiera_edulis.html |website=Desert-Tropicals |access-date=11 June 2024}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Parmentiera aculeata (Parmentiera edulis) - Fruit and Spice Park - Homestead, Florida - DSC08916.jpg|left|thumb|Foliage]]
[[File:Parmentiera aculeata.jpg|left|thumb|Flowers at various stages]]
[[File:FRUTO DE CUAJILOTE.JPG|left|thumb|Fruit]]
''P. aculeata'' is a small to medium-sized tree, typically growing to heights of around {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}}. It is evergreen to semi-deciduous. The trunk is erect and typically measures around {{convert|30|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in diameter. The bark is light brown to gray in color and is slightly [[Glossary of botanical terms#fissure|fissured]]. The young branches are [[Glossary of botanical terms#terete|terete]] and [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] to slightly [[Glossary of botanical terms#puberulous|puberulous]], and the nodes contain a thick thorn that subtends each leaf. The leaves are [[Glossary of botanical terms#opposite|opposite]] to subopposite, sometimes [[Glossary of botanical terms#alternate|alternate]], and are typically 3-[[Glossary of botanical terms#foliate|foliate]] but may occasionally be 4-foliate. The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] measure {{convert|1.3|-|3.5|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length, are narrowly winged, and have a strong groove on top. The leaflets are [[Glossary of botanical terms#entire|entire]] and [[Glossary of botanical terms#elliptical|elliptic]] to [[Glossary of botanical terms#obovate|obovate]] in shape, while the margins may be [[Glossary of botanical terms#acute|acute]] or [[Glossary of botanical terms#obtuse|obtuse]], and the bases are [[Glossary of botanical terms#cuneate|cuneate]] to [[Glossary of botanical terms#attenuate|attenuate]]. Terminal leaflets are {{convert|1.5|-|6|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length and {{convert|0.6|-|3|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in width while lateral leaflets are {{convert|1.5|-|5|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length and {{convert|0.6|-|2.5|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in width. The [[Glossary of botanical terms#petiolule|petiolules]] measure up to {{convert|1|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length.<ref name="Worldflora">{{cite web |title=Parmentiera aculeata (Kunth) Seem. |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000779463#synonyms |website=World Flora Online |access-date=13 June 2024}}</ref>

The [[inflorescences]] consist of few-flowered [[Fascicle (botany)|fascicles]] or single flowers, and are [[Glossary of botanical terms#terminal|terminal]] or [[Glossary of botanical terms#axillary|axillary]] near the branch tips, though may be borne of the nodes in older branches. The flowers are tubular, typically contain 5 [[sepals]], 4 or 5 petals, and 5 [[anthers]], and may be green, white, or purple in color. They are acute to short [[Glossary of botanical terms#acuminate|acuminate]] in their budding stage and measure {{convert|2.5|-|4|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length. The [[Glossary of botanical terms#calyx|calyces]] are [[Spathe|spathaceous]]. The [[Petal|corollas]] are [[Glossary of botanical terms#campanulate|campanulate]], {{convert|5|-|7|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length, and {{convert|2|-|2.5|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in width. The [[stamens]] are [[Glossary of botanical terms#exserted|subexserted]]. The anther [[Theca#botany|thecae]] are weakly divergent, thick, and measure {{convert|5|-|6|mm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is [[Glossary of botanical terms#oblong|oblong]] to [[Glossary of botanical terms#linear|linear]] and [[Glossary of botanical terms#lepidote|lepidote]], while the [[ovules]] are [[Glossary of botanical terms#seriate|multiseriate]].<ref name=Worldflora/>

The fruit is a large, fleshy, fibrous berry of yellow-green color, and grows directly from the trunk and branches of the tree. It is somewhat cylindrical in shape, thickly ribbed, tapered, and slightly curved. It measures {{convert|8|-|18|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length and {{convert|3|-|5|cm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in diameter, and contains numerous flat, somewhat round seeds that measure approximately {{convert|3|mm|in|abbr=off|sp=us}} in diameter.<ref name=Monaco/>

''P. aculeata'' seeds typically germinate within 1–5 weeks of planting. The tree begins flowering around 3–5 years of age.<ref name=Monaco/>

==Chemistry==
The pulp of the ripe fruit contains [[phenol]]ic compounds and exhibits [[antioxidant]] and [[antibacterial]] effects.<ref name="Phenol">{{cite journal |last1=Santiago Ruiz |first1=Cristina |last2=Nuricumbo Lievano |first2=Viviana Noemi |last3=Chapa Barrios |first3=Mariana Gabriela |last4=Vela Gutiérrez |first4=Gilber |last5=Velázquez López |first5=Arturo Alberto |title=Antimicrobial Activity, Phenolic and Antioxidant Content of Extracts from Cuajilote (Parmentiera aculeata Kunth) Fruits at Different Degrees of Ripening |journal=Journal of the Mexican Chemical Society |pages=161–169 |language=en |doi=10.29356/jmcs.v65i2.1270 |date=June 2021|volume=65 |issue=2 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The juice of the fruit was found to encourage ''[[Lactobacillus]]'' growth.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lara-Cervantes |first1=Teresa de Jesús |last2=Carrillo-Inungaray |first2=María Luisa |last3=Balderas-Hernández |first3=Victor Emmanuel |last4=Aguilar-Zárate |first4=Pedro |last5=Veana |first5=Fabiola |title=Valorization of Parmentiera aculeata juice in growth of probiotics in submerged culture and their postbiotic production: a first approach to healthy foods |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00203-022-03295-w |journal=Archives of Microbiology |access-date=14 June 2024 |pages=679 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00203-022-03295-w |date=29 October 2022|volume=204 |issue=11 |pmid=36308572 |bibcode=2022ArMic.204..679L |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

An extract from the fruit was found to induce [[diuretic]] and [[Kidney stone disease|antiurolithiatic]] effects in [[Wistar rats]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Morales-Sánchez |first1=Viridiana |last2=Osuna-Fernández |first2=Helia Reyna |last3=Brechú-Franco |first3=Alicia |last4=Laguna-Hernández |first4=Guillermo |last5=Vargas-Solís |first5=Rosario |title=Assessment of the antiurolithiatic effect of Parmentiera aculeata fruit on Wistar rat |url=https://www.botanicalsciences.com.mx/index.php/botanicalSciences/article/view/99 |journal=Botanical Sciences |access-date=14 June 2024 |pages=293–298 |language=es |doi=10.17129/botsci.99 |date=30 May 2015|volume=93 |issue=2 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[Hexane]] extract from the fruit was found to induce [[cytotoxic]] and [[apoptotic]] effects against breast cancer cell line [[MDA-MB231]]. [[MTT assay]]s conducted three days after treatment showed an [[IC50|IC<sub>50</sub>]] value of 94.63 + 1.63 μg/ml.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Estanislao Gómeza |first1=Cynthia Carolina |last2=Ordaz Pichardoa |first2=Cynthia |last3=San Martín Martínezb |first3=Eduardo |last4=Pérez Hernández |first4=Nury |last5=Pérez Ishiwara |first5=Guillermo |last6=Gómez García |first6=María del Consuelo |title=Cytotoxic effect and apoptotic activity of Parmentiera edulis DC. hexane extract on the breast cancer cell line MDA-MB-231 |url=https://japsonline.com/abstract.php?article_id=1742 |journal=Journal of Applied Pharmaceutical Science |date=2016 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=015–022 |doi=10.7324/JAPS.2016.600103 |access-date=14 June 2024|doi-access=free }}</ref>

A [[guaianolide]], [[lactucin-8-0-methylacrylate]], was isolated from the dried fruits of ''P. aculeata'' in 2000. After being administered via [[intraperitoneal injection]] to diabetic mice in amounts of 300 mg/kg, [[blood glucose]] levels decreased by 43.75%, and by 29.61% in non-diabetic mice.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pérez-Gutiérrez |first1=R. M. |last2=Pérez-González |first2=C. |last3=Zavala-Sánchez |first3=M. A. |last4=Pérez-Gutiérrez |first4=S. |title=[Hypoglycemic activity of Bouvardia terniflora, Brickellia veronicaefolia, and Parmentiera edulis] |journal=Salud Publica de Mexico |pages=354–358 |date=1998|volume=40 |issue=4 |doi=10.1590/S0036-36341998000400008 |pmid=9774905 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

''P. aculeata'' fruits contain high amounts of [[lignocellulosic]] content. Unripe fruits contain [[cellulose]] content of 42.17% and [[lignin]] content of 35.26%, while ripe fruits contain cellulose content of 32.76% and lignin content of 40.79%.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vicente-Flores |first1=Macario |last2=Güemes-Vera |first2=Norma |last3=Chanona-Pérez |first3=José Jorge |last4=Perea-Flores |first4=María de Jesús |last5=Arzate-Vázquez |first5=Israel |last6=Quintero-Lira |first6=Aurora |last7=Sánchez-Fuentes |first7=Cinthia Erika |title=doi: 10.1002/jemt.23559. Epub 2020 Sep 9. Study of cellular architecture and micromechanical properties of cuajilote fruits (Parmentiera edulis D.C.) using different microscopy techniques |journal=Microscopy Research and Technique |date=2021 |volume=84 |issue=1 |pages=12–27 |doi=10.1002/jemt.23559 |pmid=32905658 }}</ref>

==Uses==
''P. aculeata'' is planted as an ornamental, shade tree and [[live fence]] throughout its native range. Its fruits are edible and are eaten either raw or cooked, and are sometimes pickled or made into [[preserves]]. Its flavor is reportedly similar to [[sugarcane]]. They are also used as cattle [[fodder]] in southern Mexico.<ref name=Desert/>

The plant is commonly used in [[traditional medicine]]. The fruit is used to treat [[common colds]], [[diabetes]], [[asthma]], headaches, [[diarrhea]], and [[gallstones]], while the roots are used as a diuretic.<ref name=Phenol/>
